en: The Ritual for the Worship of the Buddha and Others.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
Having prostrated to the Buddha, the Lord of the World, the Lord of Speech, and also Tāriṇī;
We shall describe their sequence of worship briefly, according to the tradition. ||1||

Indeed, here, according to the sequence already described: one who has performed the going for refuge to the Three Jewels; who has obtained the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*); who has made the vow to accomplish perfect enlightenment; who possesses intense faith and a most skillful intellect; who has gone for refuge at the feet of the Guru; and who desires the welfare of sentient beings—must perform the propitiation of the Perfect Buddhas and Bodhisattvas according to the prescribed ritual. This is because the attainment of the fruits of worldly prosperity and the supreme good is preceded by that [propitiation]. According to the scriptural teaching: "One who sings the praises of the Buddha's worship is not overcome by Māras," one should first worship the Lord, the Perfect Buddha, through this sequence in order to pacify all obstacles. In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

At the end of the night, remaining on his bed and well-composed, he should, according to his own conviction, practice meditative concentration, the recitation of mantras, and the recollection of the Buddha and others. (2)

Then, having performed the cleansing of the mouth, bathing, and the washing of the hands and other limbs, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the appropriate mantras, both externally and internally, for the satisfaction of one's own self.

In this regard, the mantra for bathing is: Oṃ Āḥ Sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye Hūṃ. This same bathing mantra applies even to images and the like. Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ is the mantra for the protection of the site, oneself, and the yoga. Oṃ Hrīḥ Svāhā is the mantra for washing the hands and feet and for sipping water (ācamana). Oṃ Hūṃ is the mantra for the consecration of the seat. This procedure is also to be followed at the time of constructing a *caitya* and so forth.

Having sprinkled the ground with the mantra for purifying the earth: *oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā*, one should perform the appropriation of the site (*bhūmiparigraha*) with: *oṃ vajrabhūme hūṃ*. Having taken up cow dung and other materials with water using: *oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ svāhā*, one should begin the mandala on a clean patch of ground. *oṃ āḥ vajrarekhe hūṃ* is the mantra for the mandala. At the time of sweeping: giving is the cow dung together with water, and ethical discipline is the sweeping.
Patience is the removal of ants and termites; vigor is the undertaking of activity;
meditation is making the mind one-pointed for that moment; and wisdom is the brilliant, well-drawn lines—these very six perfections one obtains by constructing the maṇḍala of the Sage. (4)
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a splendor as radiant as the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
"Having performed bodily actions in this supreme abode of the Sugata. (5)

One should recite the praises of the maṇḍala. Then, once the sweeping is completed, one should recite: "Oṃ sva(su)rekhe, may all the Tathāgatas empower [this], svāhā! Having spoken thus, taking a single flower with the left hand, placing it upon the back of the right hand, and casting it into the maṇḍala, one should wash one's hands.

One should perform self-protection by scattering a flower on the region of one’s own head while reciting the mantra: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa 2 māṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. Having thus prepared the maṇḍala, one should visualize that maṇḍala in the form of a rising dawn-colored moon-disk and so forth, and empower it with the mantra: *oṃ candrārkavimale svāhā*.
Then, having meditated upon the goddess—the Mother of the Victors—upon the mountain endowed with continents in the center of that maṇḍala, one should worship her and her mantra. (Verse 6)
There, in Pūrvavideha, is the sage Vairocana, white in color;
he is born from the seed-syllable Oṃ and is joined with the bodhyaṅgī mudrā. ||7||
Ratnasambhava, the bestower of boons, is yellow and has the seed-syllable *trāṃ*; he resides in Jambūdvīpa.
Amitābha, the Jina, is red, has the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, and dwells in the state of meditative absorption in Godānīya. (8)
Amoghasiddhi, green in color with both hands [in the gesture of granting boons], has the seed-syllable *khaṃ* and resides in Kuru;
Akṣobhya, born from *hūṃ*, is blue, stands upon Sumeru, and is sealed with the earth-touching mudrā. (9)
Here, Vairocana is situated upon the moon, while the remaining [deities] are established upon the sun;
they possess the nature of the five wisdoms and the three bodies, are adorned with uṣṇīṣas, and are clothed in monastic robes. ||10||
All the goddesses seated upon lotuses are situated in the corner regions.
In the southeast is Locanā, white in color, born from the syllable *lāṃ*, holding a wheel, and steadfast. (11)
In the southwest is Māmakī, blue, born from *māṃ*, swift, and holding a vajra;
in the northwest is Pāṇḍarā, red, born from *pāṃ*, and possessing a red lotus.
In the northeast is Tāriṇī, dark blue in color, born from the syllable Tāṃ, seated upon a blue lotus;
she is the goddess Vajradhātvīśvarī, who abides everywhere and at all times. (13)
Therefore, its indication is not shown here separately;
rather, it is contained within that orb of the sun produced from the syllable *tha*. (14)
Yaṃ—there shall be a multicolored eight-petaled lotus; the maṇḍala, blazing with seed-syllables and their respective forms as before, should be emanated. (15)
One should worship the entire maṇḍala, which consists of the three principles (tritattva), according to the prescribed rite.
Having summoned the Jñānasattva by means of the sequence *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, the devoted person should summon, cause to enter, bind, and satisfy [the deity]. ||16||
Alternatively, one should invoke [the deities] preceded by the recitation of each individual name: *Oṃ āgaccha 2 bhagavann Akṣobhyavajra Āḥ*.
Having performed the external worship with flowers and other offerings, one should perform the mental worship.
Having performed the offering of the mandala and so forth, one should respectfully perform the praise and other rites. (17)
Therein, as for the external [offerings]:
one should first present flowers to the Lord of the Mandala with the three-syllable mantra;
thereafter, one should offer them to all [the deities] with their respective individual mantras. (18)
Having first uttered "Oṃ vajraṃ," and then [the name] beginning with "puṣpe" in the middle, one should offer it to the deities with the mantra ending in "Āḥ hūṃ svāhā. (19)

Alternatively, one should offer [the flowers] three times for each [deity] according to this sequence: Oṃ namo 'kṣobhyāya hūṃ | Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namo vairocanāya oṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namo ratnasambhavāya trāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namo 'mitābhāya hrīḥ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namo 'moghasiddhaye khaṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namo locanāyai lāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namo māmakye māṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namaḥ pāṇḍarāyai pāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Oṃ namas tārāyai tāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā || Furthermore, one should offer a greater quantity of flowers to Akṣobhya in this very same sequence: Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ svāhā.

*Oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajranaivedye hūṃ svāhā |* Thus one should present the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*). In this context, for Vairocana, there is the form of lamps and so forth; for Ratnasambhava, the fragrance of sandalwood and so forth; for Amitābha, the flavor of milk and so forth; for Amoghasiddhi, tangible objects such as clothing; and for Akṣobhya, pleasant sounds such as the lute. Having thus primarily presented these five qualities of sensory pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), one should consecrate the offering with: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmeghaprasarasamūhe sphurahi (sphuradi) maṃ gaganakaṃ hūṃ*. If one is unable [to perform physical offerings], one should perform a great mental offering (*mānasī pūjā*) as well. For example: various ornaments such as garments, banners, jewels, pearls, and necklaces; various flowers such as the lotus and water-lily; various requisites such as waist-bands, alms bowls, robes, and water-strainers; and the four continents and seven sub-continents filled with the seven precious gems and so forth—all these should be offered.
Through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment and by the force of the mantra-knowledge, and arising from my own vow within the assembly of the Perfectly Enlightened One. (20)
May clouds of offerings, established in universal auspiciousness, proceed forth;
having reflected thus with a mind that is indeed steady and diligent. (21)

Then, one should recite eight times this Queen of Great Vidyās, which effects the accomplishment of worship: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvathodgate sphurimaṃ gaganakaṃ samantataḥ svāhā*. Thereupon, clouds of unfailing offerings, as they were manifested, abide within the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are worthy of worship; however, in the case of worshiping an image, one should perform the bathing with *Oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayashriye hūṃ*, and then carry out the worship and other rites as before.

Then, I, [name], offer myself in every way and at all times to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, together with their retinues, who have entered the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). May those Great Compassionate Ones empower me, protect me, and grant me accomplishment and the supreme boon—thus is the offering of oneself.

Therefore, I confess all sins born of attachment, aversion, and delusion, occurring at all times; with those mental resolves by which the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have taught confession, with those same mental resolves I confess, just as those Blessed Buddhas know. This is the confession of sins.

Then, one should perform the rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*) as follows: "I rejoice with the unsurpassed rejoicing in all the accumulations of merit and wisdom belonging to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three times, to all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and to all sentient beings—those which purify the realm of beings, protect the realm of beings, and are both mundane and supramundane—just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know them.
Then: Homage to the Buddha, the Guru; homage to the Dharma, the Protector;
homage to the great Saṅgha; constant homage to all three. (22)
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds. I rejoice in the merit of the world and set my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha. (23)
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others. (24)
I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment;
I invite all sentient beings;
I shall practice the desired, sublime conduct of enlightenment.
"May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world. (25)
One should recite the *Triśaraṇa-gāthā*. Then, one should offer praise:

"I bow to him who, having himself awakened to Buddhahood—which is without beginning, middle, or end, and is peaceful—taught the firm and fearless path for the sake of awakening those who are unawakened."

Homage to you, who wield the sword of wisdom and compassion, the sole cutter of the sprouts of suffering held by the Vajra-Holder; you are the shatterer of the walls of doubt concealed within the thicket of various views. ||26||

Then, one should recite eight times this Queen of Vidyās, which offers an unerring hymn of praise to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: "Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! To you, the mass of those with fully blossomed supernormal knowledges everywhere, homage be to you! Svāhā!
Devotion to the Buddha, a nature free from deceit, loving-kindness toward all beings, practice in yoga, turning away from [worldly] fruits, and association with Bodhisattvas.
May I possess sharp wisdom, a body beautiful by birth within a noble family, and may I have the eloquence of a Sugata in birth after birth—enough with further elaboration! (27)

Having made such a prayer of aspiration (*praṇidhi*), one should recite this King of Mantras consisting of one hundred syllables, which possesses great merit, is the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas, and is empowered by all Buddhas:

*Namaḥ traiyadhvikānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ sarvatrāpratihatā-vāptidharmatā-balinām | Aṃ asamasamasamantato'nantatāvāptiśāsanī hara 2 smara smaraṇa vigatarāgabuddhadharmate sara sara samabalā hasa hasa traya traya gaganamahāvaralakṣaṇe jvalajvalanasāgare svāhā |* Then:
May all those throughout every direction who are afflicted by suffering of body and mind obtain oceans of happiness and joy through my merits. (28)
May the god send rain in due season, and may there be an abundance of crops;
may the world be prosperous, and may the king be righteous. ||29||
Without experiencing the suffering of the miserable realms and without the practice of austerities, may the world attain Buddhahood with a single divine body. (30)
Having recited thus, one should dedicate the merit by means of this practice of rejoicing and dedication through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). That is to say:

"In whatever way those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones know and see with their Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye—that root of virtue (kuśalamūla) which is of such a kind, of such a class, of such a nature, of such a character, and which exists according to such a true nature (*dharmatā*)—in that same way do I rejoice in that root of virtue. And in whatever way those Tathāgatas, Arhats..."
"The perfectly awakened ones authorize this dedication; I dedicate that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect awakening."

Thereafter, reciting: "Oṃ, with the graceful bows of all the Tathāgatas, I bow to the Blessed One, [the Lord] named so-and-so; Jaḥ Hūṃ Vaṃ Hoḥ! O Lord, accept this handful of flowers! Hoḥ! one should pay homage. Then:
"You have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; you have bestowed the accomplishments according to their needs. Go to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more. (31)

One should dismiss [the deities] with "Oṃ muḥ svāhā. Thereafter, one should erase the lines of the maṇḍala. Furthermore, the praise of worship has been declared by the Blessed One in the *Śraddhābalādhāna-mudrāvatāra-sūtra*.

“Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to give daily food of a hundred flavors and divine garments to as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the world-systems, and were to continue giving in this way for as many eons as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers; and suppose another son of good family or daughter of good family, Mañjuśrī, were to see a Buddha depicted in a painting, or in a book, or on a leaf—this latter person generates incalculably more merit than the former. What need is there to mention one who joins their palms in salutation, or offers a flower, or incense, or a lamp? This very person generates incalculably more merit than that.”
And in the *Śrīsamāja*: "One should always worship the Buddhas with the five qualities of sensory pleasure according to the ritual;
through the fivefold offerings of worship, one shall attain the state of Buddhahood swiftly. (32)
Whether one worships him while he is still present or when he has passed into parinirvāṇa, the merit is equal through the clarity of the mind; there is no distinction in the merit. ||33||

Even in the case of all the ritual procedures for worship, such as those of the venerable Vajrāsana Lokeśvara and others which will be described hereafter, this entire method should generally be applied; for it is uniform everywhere due to its all-pervasive nature. The only difference lies in the leader [of the mandala], his retinue, the seed-syllables, the hands, the colors, the emblems, and so forth. Oṃ.

Now, if one wishes to worship the Lord Vajrāsana, then in place of the Blessed One Akṣobhya, one should visualize upon Mount Sumeru the form of the glorious Vajrāsana. He arises from yellow seed-syllables *HŪṂ* and is presided over by those seeds. He is the transformation of a central yellow vajra, golden-hued, seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture with two arms and one face, his right hand displaying the earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśamudrā*) and his left hand resting palm-upward in his lap. His body is draped in saffron robes. He possesses a fathom-wide aura of light, is peaceful, and shines with all the marks and minor signs of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*). Having thus placed him, one should meditate on the Bodhisattva Maitreya to the right of the Blessed One; he is fair-complexioned, two-armed, wearing a crown of matted hair embracing a white reliquary (*caitya*), holding a precious fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in his right hand, and in his left, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) adorned with a cluster of *nāgakesara* flowers. Likewise, on the left, one should meditate on the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, white in color, wearing a crown of matted hair presided over by Amitābha, holding a precious fly-whisk in his right hand and a blossoming lotus surrounded by bees in his left. Both of these should be visualized as looking toward the face of the Blessed One. Then, having visualized Vairocana and the others in Pūrvavideha and the other continents as before, one should perform the offerings and so forth as previously described. This is the ritual procedure for the worship of Śrī Vajrāsana.
Now, generally speaking, if the mind is set upon the worship of the Sugata, then one should visualize that mandala as having the form of a moon-mandala.

One should bring the entire object of worship into the space of the sky as a lotus-mandala, and respectfully offer the guest-water (argha) and water for the feet (pādya) by means of one's own mantra and mudrā. (34)

*Oṃ āgaccha 2 buddhabhaṭṭāraka āḥ*. This is the invocation mantra for the Lord of Sages (*munīndra*). For other deities as well, this very same formula serves as the invocation mantra, with their respective names inserted in the middle. The syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) comes first; in the middle, "to the Buddha" (*buddhāya*) and so forth; and finally, *svāhā*. However, in the center of the mandala and in the directions starting from the east, these are the mantras for worshipping the Buddhas and others.

There, in the center of the maṇḍala: Oṃ buddhāya svāhā. In the directions beginning with the east: Oṃ kamalapāṇaye svāhā; Oṃ maitreyāya svāhā; Oṃ gaganagañjāya svāhā; Oṃ samantabhadrāya svāhā; Oṃ yakṣādhipataye svāhā; Oṃ mañjuśriye svāhā; Oṃ viṣkambhiṇe svāhā; Oṃ kṣitigarbhāya svāhā. For other venerable ones as well, the syllable *oṃ* is placed at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end within their respective names. This is the mantra for worship.
I constantly pay homage to the Buddha, who holds the excellent lotus in his hand,
whose nature is loving-kindness, who is Gaganagañja and Samantabhadra;
and to Mañjughoṣa, the lord of yakṣas, who is ever-striving for the benefit of others.
I bow with devotion to Viṣkambhin, whose body is composed of earth. ||35||
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites these names shall not enter the Avīci hell for as many eons as there are grains of sand in sixty-two Ganges rivers. The Buddha-maṇḍala is complete.

Having formed the *arghamudrā* by joining both hands in the shape of a conch shell, one should recite the mantra *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ pravarasatkāraṃ pratīccha hūṃ* and, while visualizing [the deities] before oneself, offer the *argha* three times into the receiving vessel. Then, taking a single flower with water from the *pādya* vessel with the index finger and thumb of the right hand, one should recite the mantra *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ pādyaṃ pratīccha hūṃ*. While gracefully extending the fingers beginning with the little finger and visualizing them at the feet [of the deities], one should offer the *pādya* into the second receiving vessel. [The visualizations of the deities follow: Ārya Avalokiteśvara holds a white lotus in his left hand; his crown of matted hair is graced by Amitābha. Maitreyanātha has his left hand adorned with an *aśoka* branch; his mass of matted hair is decorated with a white *caitya*. Ārya Gaganagañja is green in color and holds a golden rooster in his left hand; with his left hand, he holds a jeweled vase situated in the sky above a cloud upon a white lotus. Ārya Samantabhadra is the color of molten gold; his jewel-crown is graced by Vajrasattva, and his left hand is adorned with a radiating jewel. Ārya Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas, is dark-green in color and wears a jewel-made crown; with his left hand, he holds a vajra resting on a blue lotus. Mañjughoṣa holds a volume of the *Prajñāpāramitā* on a blue lotus in his left hand and wears a jewel-crown. Ārya Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhī is green in color and wears a jewel-crown; with his left hand, he holds a green sword resting on a white lotus. Kṣitigarbha is as white as a sea-monster (*makara*) and wears a jewel-crown; he holds a yellow eight-spoked wheel upon a white lotus. All of these are seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) on lotus-moon seats, and they grant boons with their right hands.

Now follows the worship and salutation of the glorious Bhaṭṭāraka Khasarpaṇa. Then, as before, having visualized Mount Sumeru, the four continents, and so forth within the completed maṇḍala, one should contemplate in the center, upon Sumeru, the glorious Bhaṭṭāraka Khasarpaṇa: white in color, born from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* of white hue, wearing a crown of matted hair adorned with Amitābha; granting the boon with his right hand and holding a white lotus with the other; adorned with all ornaments, his body resplendent with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs; seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) upon a moon-disc seat on a multi-petaled lotus atop a variegated jewel lion-throne, and possessing the radiance of the moon. Having thus beheld him, one should visualize Tārā and Sudhana to his right, and Bhṛkuṭī and Hayagrīva to his left. To the east, in Pūrvavideha, is Vairocana; to the south...
